planting.note: Set divisions or container-grown plants in spring into deep, humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist; protect emerging spring foliage from late frost and drying wind.

directions: Grow in partial shade in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil, mimicking the mixed deciduous and coniferous forest understory of its native Nepal and southern Tibet. The pinnately compound leaves, made up of 7-14 serrated, oblong leaflets, spread into broad clumps that make a coarse-textured companion to the more common fingered and bronze-leaf rodgersias already grown in woodland borders. Small greenish summer flowers on three-foot stalks are secondary to the bold foliage display. Give it a sheltered site away from strong wind and full sun, which can scorch the large leaflets, and divide congested clumps in early spring.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich, evenly moist soil; this scree- and streamside native tolerates drier conditions than most Petasites once established and is far less invasive.

directions: Native to limestone screes, stream margins, and unstable mountain slopes in the European Alps, this butterbur forms a well-mannered colony of large triangular leaves on stout reddish stems. In early spring, before the foliage fully unfurls, dense clusters of small, pleasantly fragrant white to pale pink flowers emerge on short stalks. Unlike the running, sometimes weedy habit of common butterbur, this alpine species stays comparatively restrained, making it suitable for a gravel-edged woodland path or rock garden margin with part-day shade. Give it gritty, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture during the growing season but good drainage, since it is adapted to scree rather than boggy ground.
